title: Modern World – I
summary: ## Decline of feudalism

Feudalism declined with the rise of the middle class, powerful kingdoms and wars between feudal lords. New towns and cities and the revival of trade gave people freedom to move and choose any profession. Money became the medium of exchange, lords accepted cash instead of services, and a powerful merchant class grew. Merchants supported strong monarchs against the feudal lords, and the feudal order broke down.
## Renaissance (14th century onwards)

Renaissance literally means 'rebirth'. It began in Italy around the 14th century AD because Italian city-states such as Venice were rich trading and intellectual centres, had political freedom and developed new commercial techniques (book-keeping, bills of exchange, public debt). The period marked the end of the Age of Faith and the beginning of the Age of Reason.

Its main ideas were humanism (faith in the creative potential of human beings), rationalism and the spirit of inquiry, with renewed interest in Classical Greek and Roman culture. The 'humanities' were born. In art, painters such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael, Botticelli and Titian painted the human body realistically; Donatello, the first great Renaissance sculptor, made the statue 'David'. Writers used vernacular languages instead of Latin, and the printing press spread their works: Dante's Divine Comedy, Erasmus's In Praise of Folly, Machiavelli's The Prince and Cervantes' Don Quixote. The Renaissance spirit also marked the rise of nationalism in Europe.
## Reformation and Counter Reformation

The medieval Catholic Church had become associated with superstition, corruption and greed. In 1517 the German priest Martin Luther challenged the Church: the Bible was the only religious authority and salvation came through faith in Christ, not through buying letters of indulgence. He was excommunicated by Pope Leo X in 1521. His Protestant Reformation divided Christians into Protestants and Roman Catholics, and spread through Henry VIII of England, Zwingli and John Calvin. In England, Henry VIII's divorce led to the Act of Supremacy, which made the King head of the Church.

The Counter (Catholic) Reformation was a reform within the Catholic Church to reduce corruption and strengthen it. It began in Spain, where Ignatius Loyola founded the 'Society of Jesus', stressing service of God, charity, chastity and missionary work.
## Development of science

Renaissance thinkers valued reason, observation and experiment over blind faith. Michael Servetus discovered the circulation of blood; William Harvey explained how the heart purifies blood and circulates it. In astronomy, Copernicus (On the Revolution of the Heavenly Sphere) argued that the earth moves round the sun; Kepler showed the planets move in elliptical orbits; Galileo, with his telescope, found the moons of Jupiter, the rings of Saturn and sunspots; Newton gave the Law of Universal Gravitation.
## Discovery of new lands

'God, Glory and Gold' drove the voyages, but the economic motive was strongest: Europeans wanted a direct sea route to the East for spices, cotton, silk and gems instead of going through Arab lands. Vasco da Gama reached India (1498), Columbus reached America, Magellan led the first voyage around the world, and Bartholomew Diaz was another famous explorer. Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal sponsored voyages. The compass, astrolabe, astronomical tables and map-making made them possible. Results: colonies in Asia, Africa and America, trade moving from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, new goods such as tobacco and potato, the cruel slave trade, and great wealth that later financed the Industrial Revolution.
## Industrial Revolution

It began in England around 1750 because English merchants had wealth from trade, colonies supplied raw materials and markets, and England had coal and iron. Machines replaced human and animal labour, but society became unequal, divided into capitalists (bourgeoisie) and workers (proletariat).
## Age of Revolutions

Glorious Revolution (1688, England): King James II lost support because of his harsh rule, an expensive standing army and the appointment of Roman Catholics. Parliament replaced him with Mary II and William III of Orange without bloodshed, ending autocracy and showing that Parliament could change the monarch.

American War of Independence: the 13 colonies suffered under Britain's mercantilist policy. The Stamp Act (1765) was opposed and repealed in 1766, but the tax on tea led to the Boston Tea Party (16 December 1773). The First Continental Congress met at Philadelphia in 1774, and the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776 stressed equality, life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. The USA was born.

French Revolution (1789): French society had three estates — Clergy, Nobility and the over-taxed Commoners. Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette had emptied the treasury. When Louis called the Estates in 1789, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen. Inspired by Voltaire, Montesquieu and Rousseau, its watchwords were Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. France became a republic under Napoleon Bonaparte. The American and French revolutions spread nationalism across the world.
## Unification of Italy and Germany

Italy was a collection of states (Venetia, Two Sicilies, Papal States, Sardinia, Tuscany). Mazzini, Garibaldi and secret societies spread the idea of unity. Piedmont-Sardinia under King Victor Emmanuel and his Prime Minister Cavour drove the Austrians out of the north; Garibaldi freed Sicily and Naples and handed them to Victor Emmanuel, who became King of Italy (1861). Rome and Venetia joined later; unification ended in 1871.

Germany was a confederation of 39 states. Bismarck, Prime Minister of Prussia under Kaiser William I, followed a 'Blood and Iron' policy and was called the 'Iron Chancellor'. He defeated Denmark (1864) with Austria, then Austria, forming the North German Confederation, and then France in the Franco-Prussian War (1871), taking Alsace and Lorraine. Germany was united under Kaiser William I and became a leading power.
## Socialism and the Russian Revolution

The Industrial Revolution created an unequal society. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels gave the ideas of socialism; in Das Capital Marx said history is the history of class struggle, and that capitalism would give way to socialism with the state owning the means of production. Russia under the autocratic Tsar Nicholas II was backward; the 1905 revolution created the Duma but little changed. Defeats in World War I, famine, inflation and the writings of Marx and Tolstoy led to strikes. In February 1917 the Tsar was deposed; in October 1917 the Bolshevik Party led by Lenin seized power. This produced the first socialist government in the world and the USSR.

sa: What is the literal meaning of Renaissance, and why did it begin in Italy in the 14th century AD?

Renaissance means 'rebirth'. It began in Italy because: (1) Italian city-states like Venice were rich trading centres where merchants brought wealth and ideas from distant lands; (2) they enjoyed political freedom and a suitable atmosphere for learning and art; (3) new commercial techniques (book-keeping, bills of exchange, public debt) brought prosperity and leisure, and the ruins of Roman buildings revived interest in classical culture.
Describe the condition of Italy on the eve of the Renaissance in the 14th century.

Italy was divided into small city-states, many built on the ruins of Roman buildings. Cities like Venice were great centres of trade and intellectual crossroads. The new political and social organisation gave freedom and a good atmosphere for academic and artistic advancement. Trade brought wealth, and people had more leisure for study.
Explain the process of the unification of Germany.

Germany was a confederation of 39 states. Kaiser William I of Prussia appointed Bismarck, who modernised the army through his 'Blood and Iron' policy. In 1864 Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark over Schleswig-Holstein; then Prussia defeated Austria and formed the North German Confederation, keeping Italy and France neutral. Finally Prussia defeated France in the Franco-Prussian War of 1871, took Alsace-Lorraine, and the remaining states joined a united Germany under Kaiser William I.
Explain the consequences of the Franco-Prussian War of 1871.

(1) France was defeated and Napoleon III abdicated. (2) France had to give up Alsace and Lorraine to Germany. (3) The southern German states joined Prussia and the unification of Germany was completed under Kaiser William I. (4) The unification of Italy was also completed, and Germany emerged as the leading power in Europe.
Analyse the contribution of Bismarck to the unification of Germany.

Bismarck, Prime Minister of Prussia, believed unity could come only by 'Blood and Iron'. He strengthened the army even against Parliament. He used diplomacy to isolate enemies — keeping Italy, France and Russia neutral — and fought three wars: against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1871). After victory over France, Germany was united under Kaiser William I; hence he is called the 'Iron Chancellor'.
What were the main causes of the American War of Independence?

(1) Britain's mercantilist policy did not allow the 13 colonies to set up industries and forced them to sell sugar, tobacco and cotton only to England at fixed prices. (2) Britain taxed the colonies to pay for its wars — the Stamp Act of 1765 and later the tax on tea, which led to the Boston Tea Party (1773). (3) The King treated the Continental Congress's appeal against 'taxation without consent' as rebellion and declared war, leading to the Declaration of Independence in 1776.
la: Explain any six major causes of the Russian Revolution.

(1) Tsar Nicholas II was an autocratic and oppressive ruler who denied people political rights. (2) Workers suffered exploitation, inhuman working conditions and heavy taxes. (3) Peasants did not get proper returns for their produce and famines worsened their condition. (4) Russia entered World War I unprepared; thousands of ill-equipped soldiers died. (5) The government printed millions of roubles, causing inflation and food shortages in cities. (6) The writings of Marx and Tolstoy awakened the workers, who formed Soviets; in February 1917 the Tsar was deposed and in October 1917 the Bolsheviks under Lenin took power.

or: Explain the socialist movement and its impact on Russia in six points.

(1) The Industrial Revolution created an unequal society of exploited workers and privileged capitalists. (2) Socialism aimed at an equal society. (3) Karl Marx and Engels said history is a history of class struggle (Das Capital). (4) Marx predicted capitalism would end and the state would own the means of production. (5) These ideas inspired Russian workers to form Soviets and demand power. (6) The October Revolution of 1917 under Lenin set up the world's first socialist government and the USSR.

la: How did the French Revolution influence the world? Explain its causes and impact.

Causes: (1) French society was divided into three estates; the clergy and nobility enjoyed privileges while the Third Estate (peasants, workers, middle class) bore heavy taxes. (2) Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette's luxury emptied the treasury. (3) In 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. (4) Thinkers like Voltaire, Montesquieu and Rousseau inspired people. Impact: (5) The Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen asserted equality, sovereignty of the people and rights to liberty, property and free speech; France became a republic. (6) Its ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, liberalism and nationalism spread across the world and inspired the unification of Italy.
What was the Reformation? Explain its causes and impact on Europe.

The Reformation was a religious and political movement that questioned the abuses of the Church. Causes: (1) the Church was associated with superstition, corruption and greed — it sold positions and letters of indulgence; (2) the Renaissance spirit of reason questioned blind faith; (3) in 1517 Martin Luther declared that the Bible was the only authority and salvation came through faith. Impact: (4) Christianity split into Protestants and Roman Catholics; (5) in England the Act of Supremacy made the King head of the Church; (6) the Catholic Church reformed itself through the Counter Reformation and the Society of Jesus.
